title: Salary CSV Upload
statement:
A small HR service keeps users as (name, salary). Staff upload a CSV file to add or update users. The upload is all-or-nothing: if any row is malformed, nothing is saved.

Write def solution(users, csv_text). users is the current DB, a list of [name, salary] with unique names. csv_text is the uploaded file. Lines are split on \n; strip each line and ignore blank ones.

  • The first non-blank line is the header row. It is always skipped and never checked, whatever it contains (the real spec says the first row is always ignored). A file with no non-blank line at all has no header row.
  • Every later line has exactly 2 comma-separated fields. The name, after stripping, is non-empty. The salary, after stripping, is a decimal number: an optional -, digits, and optionally . followed by digits (2500, 2500.50, -10). Nothing else counts, not even 1e3.
  • A file with no header row, or any malformed data row, rejects the whole file: return the string "ERROR".
  • Otherwise apply the rows in order. A row with a negative salary is skipped (it is valid, just ignored). Any other row upserts by exact name: a new name is added, an existing one is overwritten, and a later row wins over an earlier one.

Return the new DB as a list of [name, salary] sorted by name, with every salary as a float.

examples.why: Bob is overwritten, Carol is inserted, Alice keeps her salary as a float.
Dan's row is well formed but negative, so it is skipped. Skipping is not an error, so Eve is still saved.
abc is not a number, so the whole file is rejected. Dan's good row is not saved either.

constraints: names contain no commas or newlines; salaries in users are numbers ≥ 0
no quoted fields: a comma always separates fields

think.q: What are the two kinds of "bad" row, and how do they differ?
think.a: A malformed row (wrong field count, empty name, salary not a number) rejects the whole file. A negative salary row is valid but skipped. Mixing these up is the most common bug. The first row is a third case: it is the header, so it is skipped without being checked.
All rows are well formed, so apply them. Amy,100 overwrites. Amy,-5 is skipped, so Amy stays 100. Bo,7 is new. Answer [['Amy', 100.0], ['Bo', 7.0]].

think.q: What goes wrong if you write rows into the DB as you read them?
think.a: When row 900 turns out bad you have already saved 899 rows, and the file is meant to be all-or-nothing. You would need to undo them. Validate everything first, then write; in a real service this is one DB transaction.
"field", "row", "decimal number", "malformed" → string parsing with a strict validator, then a dict for the upsert. The work is careful rules, not a clever algorithm.

1. Split into stripped, non-blank lines. None left: ERROR.
  2. Drop the first line: it is the header, whatever it says.
  3. For each data line: split on ,, check 2 fields, non-empty name, decimal salary. Any failure: ERROR.
  4. Copy the DB into a dict. Apply rows with salary ≥ 0.
  5. Return sorted items as lists.

Empty file. Header only. A first row that looks like data (it is still skipped). Windows line endings (\r\n). 1e3, inf and 1. (all rejected). A blank name with a negative salary (still an error). Zero salary (kept). The same name twice.

hints: Do the work in two passes: parse_rows(csv_text) returns the rows or None, and only then do you touch the DB. That gives you all-or-nothing for free.
Do not use float() as your validator: it accepts 1e3, inf and nan. Strip an optional leading -, split on ., and check you have 1 or 2 non-empty, all-digit parts.
Use a dict for the DB: db = {name: float(s) for name, s in users}. Each row is then db[name] = salary when salary >= 0. Finish with [[n, db[n]] for n in sorted(db)].
explain:
The problem is a parser with a strict contract. The key design choice is validate first, write second: parse_rows either returns every row or None, so a bad row on line 900 cannot leave 899 rows half-saved.

  • Example 1: the header row is skipped, and both data rows pass. The dict starts as {Alice: 1000.0, Bob: 2500.0}; Bob,3000 overwrites, Carol,4000.50 inserts.
  • Example 2: Dan,-10 passes validation (it is a number) but the apply step skips it.
  • Example 3: Eve,abc fails validation, so parse_rows returns None before the DB is read.

In the real take-home this is an Express POST /upload. Say how the two passes map to a service: parse and validate the stream, then write all rows in one transaction (or one bulk upsert), so a crash mid-write also rolls back.
complexity: O(L + U log U) time for L file characters and U users after the upload, O(U) extra space for the dict

tests.label: example 1 (insert and overwrite)
tests.why: Bob is overwritten, Carol is new, Alice is untouched

tests.label: example 2 (negative salary skipped)
tests.why: Dan's row is valid but negative, so it is dropped; the rest of the file still applies

tests.label: example 3 (bad row rejects the file)
tests.why: one non-numeric salary rejects every row, including Dan's good one

tests.label: empty file
tests.why: no non-blank line, so there is no header row

tests.label: header only
tests.why: a valid file with no rows leaves the DB as it was

tests.label: header is never checked
tests.why: the first row is skipped as the header even when it has three columns

tests.label: first row looks like data
tests.why: row 1 is the header by definition, so Amy,5 is skipped and Amy keeps 1

tests.label: three fields
tests.why: every data row needs exactly two fields

tests.label: exponent is not allowed
tests.why: float() would accept 1e3, the rule does not

tests.label: blank name, negative salary
tests.why: validate first, skip second: a malformed row is an error even when its salary is negative

tests.label: same name three times
tests.why: the later valid row wins; the negative row does not overwrite

tests.label: zero salary
tests.why: zero is not negative, so it overwrites

tests.label: CRLF and blank lines
tests.why: a file saved on Windows: strip \r, skip blank lines, trim fields

args:
NAME,SALARY
Ivan,1500
Lee,-1
Jo,2200.75
Mia,999
Kai,-4100
Noor,3800
Hana,3100
tests.label: mixed upload
tests.why: overwrites, inserts and skipped negatives together

perf.label: performance: 5,000 CSV rows onto 50 users
perf.gen: [[['seed%03d' % i, i * 10] for i in range(50)], 'NAME,SALARY\n' + '\n'.join('emp%03d,%d' % ((i * 7919) % 200, (i * 37) % 6000 - 500) for i in range(5000))]

govtech.evidence: A 2025 copy of the take-home spec (github.com/bryanlohxz/swe-take-home-assignment, which says it is adapted from GovTech ACE hiring) and a candidate's March 2025 solution (github.com/tjingsheng/swe-take-home-assignment) define POST /upload for a NAME,SALARY CSV whose first row is always ignored, where an unparseable salary or a wrong column count rejects the whole file, negative salaries are skipped and existing names are replaced; this is that rule set as one timed function, with the strict number format chosen for this exercise.
extensions: The file is 10 GB. You cannot hold it in memory, but it is still all-or-nothing. Stream it line by line into a staging table, then swap or merge inside one transaction. The take-home README itself asks about long-running uploads.
Two staff upload files that touch the same names at the same time. What does each see? Discuss one transaction per upload, row locks or INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, and which upload should win.
Return a useful error instead of "ERROR": the line number and reason of the first bad row, e.g. line 4: salary "abc" is not a number. Count lines before you drop blank ones.
Support quoted fields such as "Tan, Ah Kow",3000. A plain split(',') breaks; use the csv module or a small state machine that tracks whether you are inside quotes.
